newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Internet opens up secret world of medicine.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Internet opens up secret world of medicine.

text.p: When Robin Jutzi was growing up, cystic fibrosis was no big deal. Two of his brothers had it and taking pills was a family ritual, not a trauma.
But when his brothers died, he felt he had nowhere to turn -- until he found the Internet. Now he "speaks" regularly with other adults living with the chronic disease.

The Internet -- specifically the "world wide web" of electronic mail, bulletin boards and live forums that connects personal and institutional computers -- has transformed the way people all over the world deal with health issues.
"CF (cystic fibrosis) wasn't anything special, growing up. All the pills and therapies were just normal," Jutzi, 37, said in an interview conducted over the Internet.
"It was weird that other people didn't have to do all that stuff. I still look across at my wife at suppertime and think it's really strange that she doesn't take enzymes with her meal."
But his feeling of being normal disappeared after first one and then the other brother succumbed to the incurable illness, which causes lung and intestinal damage.
"I have felt unbearably lost and alone, really having to confront the loss of the only two people in the world who really have a clue about what I live through," he said.
"Then late last fall, I got my modem fixed."

The modem gave Jutzi, an English professor in North Bay, Ontario, a telephone connection to the Internet and sites that offer medical information, advertisements about products, and bulletin boards for the latest news and gossip.

"A whole new world opened up to me...a community that spoke the same language, that generally had the same warped sense of humour. I felt at home. I got to know, intimately, people I had never met, from different cultures around the world."
John Tatton, whose six-year old son has cystic fibrosis, is more interested in getting medical information about the condition.
"The 'traditional' or main electronic and print media normally don't report the day-to-day activities in research fields," he complained.

"Unless a significant breakthrough is made they tend to ignore or relegate them to the back pages. To people afflicted with genetic diseases, cystic fibrosis etc, the small advancements in genetic research and testing may provide hope, and that is all they have."
There are literally hundreds of sites people like Tatton can look at. Some contain information from medical journals; others summarise conference proceedings.
DOCTORS NO LONGER HOLD ALL THE CARDS
Many of the Internet browsers find their new-found knowledge gives them a better background for dealing with the once-mysterious medical profession.
"It gives me back-up information to ask questions of the doctors," said Agnes Moore, a Canadian whose 10-year-old son has cystic fibrosis.

For her, the word of a doctor is no longer the ultimate authority. "If tests are ordered or questioned, I can get comparative information from members of the group. So far virtually all of the information appears to be authentic and accurate," she said.

"I not only get the practical support of finding out information -- asking what needs to be asked and getting answers within 24 hours -- but there seems to be a good deal of emotional support in the sense that others are experiencing similar challenges."

Mike Sangregorio searches for information about his heart disease. "My wife was just told she may have osteoporosis and the Internet will be the first place I will go for more information," he said. "I have no doubt I will find what I am looking for there."
"It is like having access to thousands of libraries with millions of books all at the touch of a few keys," enthused Fernando Morales De La Cruz, a Guatemalan journalist.
People with HIV or AIDS were one of the first groups to get organised on the Net.

"We believe the HIV/AIDS population has led the way in changing the physician-patient relationship, through maximum preparation for the clinical encounter and the evolution of the role of patient as advocate," said Jamie Marks, president of the New York-based Body Health Resources Corporation, which runs a very popular HIV site.
"Do we find people become more informed/empowered when they talk to their doctors after visiting our site? Definitely."
Doctors have recognised this too, and many give patients with HIV an active role in determining what their treatment should be.
ATTITUDES HAVE BEEN TRANSFORMED
Marks, who says his site is used by 50,000 people a month, sees a huge transformation in attitudes about who is in control of health care.

"What started as a reaction to the perceived prejudice and slow response of the medical establishment regarding AIDS has now become a trend in health care generally -- pushing to receive the best possible care," he said.
Health professionals use it, too, but sometimes worry about the quality of information. Some of the forums, they complain, amount to little more than gossip sessions.
"I am a strong advocate of the use of e-mail discussion forums," said Bryan Iverson, a pharmacist in Stettler, Alberta in Canada.
Iverson noted that no one screens what goes on the Internet, and desperate people grasping at any bit of information could become misinformed.
"My best advice to patients is to read as much as possible, from all sources (and) use the information to initiate discussion with medical staff," he said
PROFESSIONALS BENEFIT, TOO
The Net can also provide life-saving information to professionals.
Dr Praveen Aggarwal of the All India Institute of Medical Science in New Delhi, posted a plea for help on the Federation of American Scientists' Program for Monitoring Emerging Diseases (ProMED).
"We are facing a near-epidemic of dengue haemorrhagic fever in Delhi, India," he wrote.
"Despite managing these patients on the lines stated in textbooks, many of our patients are dying. I wonder whether we are erring somewhere in diagnosis and management of these patients."
Did anyone answer his plea?
"Yes, Dr Aggarwal received the help he needed within hours," said Jack Woodall, Director of ProMED-mail at the New York State Department of Health.
